name: Kira Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at eight at Eastgate, which is a community health centre on the east side of the city, mostly people on low pay and a lot of families who arrived in the last few years. I see a patient every ten or fifteen minutes until lunch, then paperwork or a home visit, then another clinic until six. I'm still slow, honestly. I check almost every new prescription with Dr Okafor, my supervisor, and I run late most afternoons.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the regulars, like the old man who brings me a lemon from his tree every time he comes in about his blood pressure. What wears me out is the screen. Half my day is typing notes and referral letters, and the clinic keeps asking us to try this AI note-taker, which I won't touch. Then I go home to my partner Tomas, who teaches music at a secondary school, and we both complain about our managers over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly, I told you so. I'd post something about how the money spent on AI pilots should have gone on more nurses and longer appointments. At work I'd tell Wendy, our practice nurse, that we can finally stop pretending a chatbot is going to fix the waiting list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is safe in that world, and I know my pay is good and I've got savings. But Eastgate is still underfunded, the waiting list is still six weeks, and I'm still going home at seven with notes unfinished. AI Plateau doesn't make any of that better, it just means nobody can blame the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do now, typing my own notes and getting quicker at them. I'd join the junior doctors' committee of the union this winter, because the real fight is about staffing, not software. And I'd keep putting the rent from my gran's old flat into savings, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, a bit smug, and still tired. Relieved for the patients, mostly. Tired because the problems I actually have don't go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the waiting list stays at six weeks. What does that look like on a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday I had ten minutes with a woman who'd waited five weeks to talk about a lump. No AI tool fixes that, only more doctors and more time. I ran twenty minutes over and the rest of the afternoon was a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the reception team, because even in the boring version the managers want an automatic booking system to take the phones. Sandra on reception has been there nineteen years and knows every family by name. If anyone loses hours when nothing much changes, it's her, not me.

say: AI Plateau shows the **AI pilots** were money that should have gone on nurses and longer appointments.
I'd tell colleagues we can stop pretending a **chatbot** will fix the waiting list.
think: My **job and pay** are safe here, and my savings mean money isn't the worry.
Eastgate stays **underfunded**, with six-week waits and notes I finish at home.
Nobody can blame robots any more, so the **staffing problem** is plain to see.
do: Keep typing my own **notes** and work on getting faster at them this year.
Join the union's **junior doctors' committee** this winter to push for staffing.
Keep putting the **rent** from Gran's old flat into savings each month.
feel: **Relieved** for the patients and a little smug that the hype failed.
Still **tired**, because the real problems at the clinic don't go away.
S0.quote: Last Thursday I had ten minutes with a woman who'd waited five weeks to talk about a lump. No AI tool fixes that, only more doctors and more time.
fieldNote: She is **financially secure** but already worn down by workload, so even the quiet world carries strain.
Her anger points at **funding and managers**, not at the technology itself.
She worries more about **reception staff** losing hours than about herself.

steps.text: Keep writing her own patient notes and refuse the AI note-taker
Join the medical union's junior doctors' committee this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the staff meeting: if the AI writes our letters and books our patients, the time saved has to go back to patients, not into more appointments per hour. Online I'd share the union's line on that. I'd say I'm not anti-technology, I'm anti-cutting-corners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared I'd be the one who looks slow. Everyone else would be using the AI note-taker and the referral writer, and I'd be the junior still typing, seeing fewer patients. My contract at Eastgate comes up for renewal next autumn, and a manager with a spreadsheet would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get rules into our contract: no patient talks to a chatbot without being told, and no doctor is judged on speed alone. I'd write to our local representative about AI triage in public clinics. I'd sit the clinic's training on the note-taker, because I'd have to, but I'd still check every word it wrote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground is moving and I'm the only one standing still on purpose. I'm proud of that and also a bit embarrassed by it. Mostly I feel tense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check every word the note-taker wrote. Wouldn't that make you even slower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably, and I know that's a contradiction. But I've seen one of these tools write that a patient denied chest pain when she never said a word about her chest. If my name is on the note, I'm checking it, even if it costs me five minutes a patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner the night the renewal letter came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas I'd rather move to another clinic than be measured like a call centre. There are three other practices within a bus ride of our flat, so I'd have options. Being twenty-seven with savings and no kids means I can afford to be stubborn, and I know not everyone can.

say: Time the AI saves must go **back to patients**, not into more appointments per hour.
I'm not against technology, I'm against **cutting corners** with patients' care.
think: I'm afraid I'll look like the **slow junior** still typing while others use the tools.
My **contract renewal** next autumn makes speed figures matter more than they should.
do: Push the union for **contract rules** on AI use and how doctors are measured.
Write to my **local representative** about chatbot triage in public clinics.
Sit the compulsory **note-taker training** but check every word it writes.
feel: **Tense** and stubborn, proud of standing still but a bit embarrassed by it.
S1.quote: Being twenty-seven with savings and no kids means I can afford to be stubborn, and I know not everyone can.
fieldNote: She admits the **contradiction** of checking AI notes so carefully that she gets slower still.
Her **savings** give her the freedom to refuse, and she sees that as a privilege.
Her backup plan is **another clinic** nearby, not leaving medicine.

steps.text: Push the union to add AI and speed rules to her contract
Write to her local representative about chatbot triage in clinics
Sit the clinic's compulsory training on the AI note-taker
Apply to one of three nearby clinics if her renewal goes badly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster for patients and that health care should be the last place handed over to a machine. I'd be loud about it, at work and online, and I'd join every campaign that wanted a human doctor guaranteed in public clinics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think junior doctors like me go first. If the AI can take a history and make a diagnosis better than me by 2028, a manager will ask why they need a doctor who still checks her prescriptions with her supervisor. The nurses would do the hands-on bits until 2031, and I'd be paid to sign things, if I'm paid at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd move my training towards hands-on work: coil fitting, joint injections, minor surgery, things a robot can't do until about 2031. I'd ask Dr Okafor to sign me off on procedures this year. I'd keep at least a year of money in the bank and stop any big spending, and I'd push hard through the union for a law that a person signs every diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I spent six years training for this, and the idea that it's worth almost nothing by the time I'm twenty-nine is hard to sit with. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would you change that, with two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know that's stubborn. Learning to use the AI that replaces me feels like digging my own grave neatly. I'd rather spend the two years getting good with my hands, because that buys me three more years before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him his teaching job might outlast my doctoring, which is a strange thing to say out loud. I'd say we should keep the flat small and not buy anything. And I'd tell him I'm not giving up, I'm just moving to the parts of medicine that need hands.

say: Health care should be the **last place** handed over to a machine.
I'd back every campaign for a **human doctor** guaranteed in public clinics.
think: **Junior doctors** like me go first once AI diagnoses better than we do by 2028.
I'd end up **signing things** for a machine, if I'm paid at all.
do: Train in **hands-on procedures** like coil fitting and joint injections this year.
Keep at least **a year of money** in the bank and stop big spending.
Push the union for a law that a **person signs** every diagnosis.
feel: **Sick** and sleepless at the thought that six years of training lose their value by 29.
S2.quote: Learning to use the AI that replaces me feels like digging my own grave neatly.
fieldNote: She sees her job as mostly **thinking work**, so the 2028 date hits her directly.
She still **refuses AI tools**, even with only two years' warning.
The **three-year gap** before robots is her whole plan: get skilled with her hands fast.

steps.text: Get signed off this year on coil fitting, joint injections and minor surgery
Keep a full year of living costs in the bank
Campaign through the union for a law that a doctor signs every diagnosis

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before: patients deserve a human being, and the government has five years to write that into law. I'd say it calmly, at the clinic and online, because with five years you can actually win an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes a lot for me. I'd be thirty-two, I could finish my specialist training in family medicine and add procedures, and I'd be a senior doctor rather than a junior. Seniors who do hands-on work have until about 2034 before robots catch up, so I think I'd still lose part of my work, but not all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the specialist training programme next year instead of waiting. I'd build up the procedures side, maybe sexual health and women's health, where people really want a person in the room. I'd stay active in the union and keep saving the rent from the flat, so that by 2031 I've got two years' cushion instead of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not sick like with the two-year one. It feels like a race I could run. I'd still think about it every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the clinic look like in 2031 in this picture, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess the AI does the first conversation with most patients, and the doctors left are the ones who do procedures and the hard cases. If the clinic cuts from nine doctors to five, I want to be one of the five, and five years is enough time to become one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Eastgate you'd worry about in that version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dr Patel, who's fifty-eight and does almost no procedures, would be in trouble, though he might just retire. And the reception team again. I think about Sandra more than I think about myself, honestly, because she has no savings and no degree to fall back on.

say: Patients deserve a **human doctor**, and government has five years to put that in law.
With five years' warning, we can **win the argument** if we start now.
think: By 2031 I'd be **thirty-two** and a trained senior, not the junior who goes first.
I'd still **lose part** of my work, but hands-on skills buy time until 2034.
do: Apply for **specialist training** in family medicine next year instead of waiting.
Build up **women's and sexual health** procedures, where patients want a person present.
Save the flat's rent to reach **two years** of cushion by 2031.
feel: **Worried** every week, but it feels like a race she could actually win.
S3.quote: If the clinic cuts from nine doctors to five, I want to be one of the five, and five years is enough time to become one.
fieldNote: Five years turns her mood from **dread to effort**, because training can be finished in time.
She expects **fewer doctors** per clinic and wants to be among those kept.
Her concern keeps returning to **staff without degrees**, like the receptionist.

steps.text: Apply for family medicine specialist training next year and add procedures
Save the flat's rent to reach two years of living costs by 2031
Stay active in the union's campaign for a human doctor in clinics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have ten years, so there's no excuse for not having proper rules. I'd want the medical union, patient groups and government sitting down now, before the tech firms write the rules for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, the next few years look fine. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, a qualified family doctor with procedures and probably a list of patients who know me. The thinking side of my job would go in 2036 and robots would come for the rest around 2039, so I'd have time to plan, but I'd still only be in my early forties when it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my training at a normal pace and not panic. I'd stay in the union and push for a plan for doctors in the 2030s, like guaranteed retraining. And by the early 2030s I'd look at teaching medical students on the side, because teaching people to examine a patient feels like something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still uneasy, because the end point is the same and I don't like where it ends. But ten years feels like a career, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said early forties when it all lands. What would that mean for you and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably want kids in the early 2030s, so I'd be a doctor with a small child when the AI arrives. That's when I'd want the savings big and the mortgage small. I'd rather know that now than find out at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd never use AI tools. With ten years, does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, by the end. If it's been safe in other clinics for years, I might use it for the referral letters. But I'd never let a computer be the one who tells a patient they have cancer, not in 2036 or ever.

say: Ten years leaves **no excuse** for not having proper rules in place.
Unions, patient groups and government should set rules **before tech firms** do.
think: The **next few years** look fine, and I'd be a qualified doctor by 2036.
The end point still lands in my **early forties**, maybe with a small child.

Push the union for **guaranteed retraining** for doctors in the 2030s.
Start **teaching medical students** on the side by the early 2030s.
feel: **Calmer**, because ten years feels like a career rather than a cliff.
Still **uneasy** about where it ends, even with time to plan.
S4.quote: I'd never let a computer be the one who tells a patient they have cancer, not in 2036 or ever.
fieldNote: Ten years moves her **worry** from her own job to the timing of a future family.
She softens slightly on **AI for letters**, but draws a hard line at giving bad news.
She sees **teaching hands-on skills** as work that might last.

steps.text: Finish specialist training at a normal pace and keep her Eastgate patients
Push the union for guaranteed retraining for doctors in the 2030s
Start teaching medical students how to examine patients by the early 2030s

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to finish training or change anything, and I'd be the junior nobody needs. What would help is a law that a human doctor signs off every diagnosis, and paid time to train in procedures, funded by the health service, not by me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients much. Most people at Eastgate don't have a smartphone with data, or they don't read the language well. If the plan is a chatbot for the poor and a human doctor for the rich, I'd fight that harder than anything about my own job.

headlineQuote: If the plan is a chatbot for the poor and a human doctor for the rich, I'd fight that harder than anything about my own job.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at Eastgate, a busy community health centre serving low-income and migrant families.
She has **strong savings** plus rent from her gran's old flat, and lives with Tomas, a music teacher.
She **refuses AI tools** and blames managers and funding, not technology, for her clinic's problems.
Her mood climbs from **uneasy to alarmed** in the two-year AGI picture, where she expects juniors to go first.
Her answer is always **union action** plus moving into hands-on procedures that robots reach later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to finish training and juniors would be cut first.
whatWouldHelp: A law that a **human doctor** signs off every diagnosis.
Paid, **health-service-funded** time to train in hands-on procedures.
